Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya with Redwood, and Jonah is our SE. Are you all seeing the deck?
[00:06] Sarah: Yeah we can see it, Maya. Thanks. Quick note, we scheduled 45 but 42 is fine, we know people have tight schedules.
[00:12] Jonah: Great, I'll try to keep the deep stuff focused. We know BlueHeron cares about latency for patient chat and also strict handling of PHI.
[00:18] Dr. Luis: Yep PHI is the main constraint; we want to keep as little user data stored as possible, and auditability is a must.
[00:25] Maya: Totally understood. Today we'll demo hosted chat gen — streaming behavior and how to tune params for cost/latency, then retry/backoff patterns and a quick Console tour for Optimize recommendations.
[00:34] Priya: Can you also cover how Redwood handles KV cache? We saw notes about K-V cash in the docs and want to know if that's retained. (laugh)
[00:41] Jonah: Good question, yes we — sorry the transcript reads K V cash sometimes — we call it KV cache, it's in-memory per-request and can be configured. For hosted, default is ephemeral and not persisted to disk.
[00:53] Sarah: So by default hosted API does not keep PHI beyond request lifetime?
[00:57] Maya: Correct, hosted default retention is minimal; we can also enable customer-managed keys for encryption at rest. We'll include SOC2 details in the packet.

[01:10] Jonah: Alright, quick demo. I'm switching to the sandbox and will start a streaming chat call. I'm going to use a small system prompt and then stream a user question about medication interactions. You'll see tokens arrive incrementally.
[01:22] [Jonah shares screen: terminal -> curl streaming example]
[01:28] Jonah: Here is the command, note the stream=true flag, and a max_tokens=256. If you set temperature low, outputs are deterministic; higher temp gives more diversity but you pay for extra tokens if it rambles.
[01:40] Maya: A lot of engineering teams mix up top_p and temperature; Jonah, maybe show an example where top_p=0.9 vs temp=0.8.
[01:47] Jonah: Sure. Running with temp 0.2 first. (typing) You can see the latency per first byte is ~80ms in this sandbox region.
[01:56] Sarah: 80ms first byte is good. Our product target is sub-200ms for first-word in chat.
[02:02] Jonah: Important note: first-token latency depends on model size, route selection, and batching. Our Console traces show per-token timing and you can set routing policy to pick low-latency replicas.

[02:18] [02:18] Maya: Let's intentionally trigger a transient failure to show retry behavior. Jonah, can you simulate a 503?
[02:24] Jonah: Yep. I'll toggle backoff example: client sends with idempotency token header; if the server returns 5xx, client will retry with exponential backoff up to X times. We're streaming so you have to be careful about partially streamed responses.
[02:36] Priya: How do you handle partial streams? If a retry happens, will the client receive duplicate tokens?
[02:40] Jonah: Good — we recommend an idempotency key per user-turn and a sequence-numbering approach. On the server we can resume by storing KV cache entries keyed to the idempotency token for a short window. That avoids duplicates. In hosted mode the default TTL for those cache entries is short but configurable for Dedicated.
[02:56] Dr. Luis: Is that persisted to customer storage or Redwood-managed?
[02:59] Jonah: Redwood-managed ephemeral for hosted; in Private/Dedicated we can integrate with your storage/KMS.

[03:08] [03:08] Maya: Now back to parameters — max_tokens, stop sequences. For patient-facing flows you often want to cap length to avoid hallucination and cost spikes. Also use stop tokens to prevent wandering.
[03:18] Sarah: We're worried about hallucinations around drug names. Any guardrails?
[03:22] Jonah: Two approaches: 1) Constrain generation via structured outputs and use function/tool calling to validate against a drug database. 2) Monitor quality with Redwood Optimize — it can suggest lowering temperature and adding domain-specific stop prompts, and will alert on QA regressions tied to a prompt set.
[03:37] Priya: Is Optimize integrated in the Console?
[03:39] Maya: Yes, Optimize surfaces suggestions and simulates expected cost changes; it's visible in the Console under the 'Optimize' tab. We'll show that in a sec.

[03:50] [03:50] Jonah: Switching to Console — here's a per-route dashboard, token breakdown, p50/p95 latencies, and a set of suggestions: batch window shorten, enable prefix caching, quantize model to int8 for cost savings. These are advisory but you can apply them to sandbox routes.
[04:07] Sarah: Quantization for hosted? I thought that was only for private deployments.
[04:11] Jonah: We run quantized variants for many hosted model instances; the console labels the model variant. For strict compliance you might prefer dedicated nodes — that's in the Dedicated product line. We'll outline the tradeoffs in the follow-up doc.

[04:24] [04:24] Maya: Quick lightning Q&A before we demo a failure and retry pattern live.
[04:28] Sarah: Timeline question — we are planning a limited pilot in Q3; will hosted suffice for pilot?
[04:33] Maya: Generally yes for pilot — hosted gives quick onramp. For production with PHI you often transition to Dedicated or Private depending on audit needs; we help with that migration path.
[04:43] Dr. Luis: What about SSO / SAM-el integration? (laughter) Sorry, SAM-el..
[04:47] Jonah: (laugh) We support SAML/SAML 2.0 and OIDC, and RBAC in the Console. We'll include our SSO setup guide.

[05:00] [05:00] Jonah: Now I'm going to simulate a transient capacity error and show the recommended client-side handling. I'm issuing 5 quick concurrent streaming requests and throttling one to return 429.
[05:12] [05:12] System: slight audio overlap / crosstalk
[05:15] Jonah: Here the client sees 429 with Retry-After header. Redwood SDKs will backoff and retry respecting idempotency token. For streaming we recommend chunk checkpointing and re-requesting missing segments, or graceful fallback to a smaller model so you don't block the user.
[05:32] Priya: So fallback model is automatic?
[05:34] Jonah: You can configure routing policy to fallback to a cheaper model in the same family — Console lets you set priority lists per route.
[05:41] Sarah: Will that change output style and break UX?
[05:44] Jonah: It can; Optimize can run A/B checks and flag regressions. For critical flows we recommend mapping variants and adding a small post-processing normalization step to align tone.

[05:58] [05:58] Maya: A quick note on cost controls — set per-route quotas and token caps; console alerts when a route exceeds expected token spend. For healthcare it's often useful to run a preflight check to ensure tokens per convo stay within budget.
[06:12] Dr. Luis: Can we set retention = 0 for hosted? We need no retention of logs.
[06:16] Maya: By default Redwood retains minimal logs for debugging; you can request stricter retention and we can enable log redaction or direct logs to your Cloud Storage in Private options. We'll put the exact retention options in the security doc.

[06:30] [06:30] Jon — sorry Jonah: (small laugh)
[06:32] Jonah: No worries. Last part — demo a long-running stream where we show how the client handles partial failure and resume. I'm going to start a 1200-token test and simulate a network drop after 400 tokens.
[06:43] [06:43] Jonah runs test; partial stream visible
[06:50] Jonah: When the client reconnects with the same idempotency token, the server recognizes the prior session and resumes from the last KV cache point — you may see a small overlap or continuation depending on TTL. We log an event in the Console trace.
[07:05] Priya: How long is that TTL?
[07:08] Jonah: Default ephemeral window in hosted is 30s to 2min depending on plan; Dedicated gives you longer control.

[07:15] Sarah: If we need guaranteed no duplication, recommend what?
[07:18] Jonah: Use explicit sequence numbers returned by the server and client-side dedupe on the application layer; Redwood's SDKs expose helpers for this. We'll attach sample code.

[07:28] [07:28] Maya: We're running short on time — quick recap and explicit next steps.
[07:31] Sarah: Quick follow-up: is there a direct compliance questionnaire we can start with for our procurement?
[07:35] Maya: Yes, we'll send the vendor security questionnaire and SOC2 type II report. That's part of the packet.
[07:40] Dr. Luis: Also want the benchmark — can you run a 1k concurrent short convo run to measure p95?
[07:44] Jonah: Yep I'll run that in our staging region and share CSVs and traces.
[07:48] Priya: And sandbox access — please invite engineering so we can start implement tests.
[07:52] Maya: Will do.

[08:00] [08:00] Closing minutes — casual administrative notes, a couple of quick clarifications about pricing tiers and a mention of Dedicated SLA windows.
[08:12] Sarah: Thanks both, the demo was useful. We'll look for the docs.
[08:16] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll send notes and the security packet.
[08:20] [Speaker 1]: End of recording.

Notes about transcription: occasional mishearings (SAML as SAM-el, KV cache as K V cash), some crosstalk around the simulated failure.
